newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets revel in status quo after elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets revel in status quo after elections.

text.p: Market players breathed a collective sigh of relief after voters on Tuesday preserved the split Washington lineup that has overseen steady, if unspectacular, U.S. economic growth and a shrinking federal budget deficit.
Stocks posted big gains Wednesday, with the Dow Jones industrials rising 54.42 points to 6,135.60 in late morning.
Bonds see-sawed, consolidating Tuesday's sharp gains, before the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rose 5/32 to 102-09/32. Its yield sank to 6.57 percent, an eight-month low.

Democratic President Bill Clinton easily turned back Republican challenger Bob Dole Tuesday, but the GOP held on to small majorities in both houses of Congress, setting the stage for continuing moderation in fiscal policy, analysts said.

"That certainly has been a good recipe for the financial markets. This group seems to fight a lot about deficit reduction, but they have actually gotten things done," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
Last week the White House trumpeted a drop in the federal deficit to a 15-year low at $107.3 billion in fiscal year 1996 from 1995's $163.9 billion.
Meanwhile, the markets have generally applauded Clinton economic appointees for their deft handling of the economy.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, first selected by ex-President Ronald Reagan and later renominated by President George Bush and Clinton, is a Wall Street darling.
Republican control of the Senate, which must confirm White House appointees, was considered a major factor in Clinton's decision to keep Greenspan when his term expired last March.

"Republicans are much more supportive of the Fed than Democrats, and the Fed's successful monetary policy has brought down inflation and interest rates--the fundamental force behind the stock market's strength, said Tim McGee, economist at Tokai Bank.
Simliarly, Clinton's Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin gets widespread praise for rescuing the dollar from historic lows last year.
Rubin reversed the course of his predecessor, Lloyd Bentsen, by carefully advocating a "strong" dollar and engineering well-timed open market forays to aid the greenback.
"The Clinton Administration, since Rubin came on board, has inspired confidence in the currency," Berner said.
After rallying Tuesday as the outcome of the elections became clear, the dollar dipped on profit taking Wednesday but stayed near 114 yen, just below last week's 42-month high.
Stock market pros also celebrated the defeat of California initiative Proposition 211, which would have made it easier for shareholders to sue companies over poor stock performance.
"People were worried going into that, especially with the (small-capitalization technology) stocks," said Stan Shipley, senior market strategist at Lehman Brothers.
The Nasdaq composite index, loaded with stocks of California technology companies, rose 10.46 points to 1,239.48 on Wednesday.

Legislators have helped promote market optimism, with many sounding conciliatory themes in the wake of the split elections. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have pledged to work together to keep shrinking the budget deficit.

"We've got a president that has said a lot of the same things that Republicans have been saying for years and so there's a lot of mutual goals between the president and most all of the Republican memebers," said House Budget Committee member Nick Smith, R-Mich., in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
